Adsorbent / material: Corn-stalk biochar (CS), wheat-straw biochar (WS), lignin-impregnated CS-L and WS-L
Experimental design / conditions: Pristine feedstocks rinsed with deionized water, oven-dried at 100 °C for 24 h, size fraction 0.15–0.38 mm, pyrolysed from 25 to 600 °C at 20 °C/min and held at 600 °C for 5 h. For impregnation, 1 g lignin per 100 mL water; 1 g char contacted with 100 mL lignin solution for 24 h at 25 °C, then washed, dried at 100 °C for 24 h and calcined at 600 °C for another 5 h.
Reported result: Lignin impregnation is a second-stage aqueous impregnation and calcination process, not a minimal modification.
Value / units: 600 °C, 5 h initial pyrolysis; 1 g lignin/100 mL; 24 h impregnation; 600 °C, 5 h second calcination
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Additional lignin, water, washing, drying and second heating are process burdens; no yield, reagent recovery, cost or LCA reported in the main article.

Experimental design / conditions: Table 1 compares BET-specific surface area, total pore volume (TPV), average pore size and point of zero charge (pHPZC).
Reported result: SSA values were CS 211.55, WS 123.84, CS-L 334.19 and WS-L 478.39 m²/g; TPV 0.1370, 0.1349, 0.1998 and 0.3087 cm³/g, respectively. pHPZC values were 8.23, 8.41, 8.35 and 8.52.
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Do not equate higher BET area alone with practical superiority; the authors' own correlation analysis found TPV related more strongly to observed capacity than SSA (reported R² values: SSA 0.3958; internal SSA 0.4400; TPV 0.6730; average pore size 0.0136; PDF p. 4, Fig. S1 referenced).

Experimental design / conditions: Figure 2 reports the adsorption capacities for the four materials; the main text attributes stronger uptake on WS and WS-L to their measured pore properties.
Reported result: Reported capacities: CS 13.30 mg/g; WS 16.63 mg/g; CS-L 21.48 mg/g; WS-L 31.48 mg/g. WS-L was reported as 1.89 times the corresponding pristine wheat-straw biochar capacity.
Model / metric: Reported observed/experimental adsorption-capacity values in Fig. 2; not table-S3 fitted Langmuir qmax
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 4, Fig. 2 and adjacent discussion; abstract on p. 1
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: The Fig. 2 caption itself does not list operating conditions. Methods describe separate kinetics tests at 15 mg/L TCH, 100 mg char/L, 25 °C, 150 rpm and sampling through 72 h; keep the Fig. 2 values tied to their actual figure context and do not silently call them fitted qmax.

Experimental design / conditions: Kinetics: 100 mg biochar in 1 L of 15 mg/L TCH, 25 °C, 150 rpm, up to 72 h, triplicates. Isotherms: 5 mg in 50 mL at initial TCH 1–15 mg/L and 5, 15, 25, 35 or 45 °C. pH tests varied pH 3–11. Cation tests used 0.02–0.1 mol/L of Na+, K+, Ca2+, Mg2+ or Al3+.
Reported result: Pseudo-first/second-order fits were reported with R² 0.9264–0.9890; PSO fit better for pristine CS/WS, PFO for CS-L/WS-L. Langmuir fits were reported with R² 0.9751–0.9952. TCH adsorption peaked at pH 7; Na+, K+, Mg2+ and Al3+ suppressed uptake as concentration increased, whereas Ca2+ increased uptake, attributed to Ca–TCH complexation.
Value / units: R² kinetic fits 0.9264–0.9890; Langmuir fits 0.9751–0.9952; optimal reported pH 7
Model / metric: Empirical kinetic/isotherm models and factor-response trends; numerical qmax in Table S3 not available in the supplied PDF
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 2, 5–6; §2.3; Fig. 5; Tables S1–S3 are referenced but not supplied
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Model-fit preference is not proof of a unique mechanism. Supporting Information is not included in this upload, so detailed kinetic/isotherm parameter tables cannot be verified. The experiments use deionized water, not a demonstrated real wastewater sample.

Experimental design / conditions: FTIR changes after adsorption and pH/cation response were used to infer pore filling, π–π interactions, hydrogen bonding and electrostatic interactions.
Reported result: Authors infer mainly physical adsorption associated with pore filling and other interactions. The actual paper's methods use deionized-water solutions, despite abstract wording that refers to adsorption in wastewater.
Value / units: Qualitative mechanism; no separately quantified mechanism contribution
Model / metric: Mechanistic inference from FTIR, pH and cation-response experiments
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 7, §3.5 and conclusions; methods on pp. 2–3
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Critical scope caveat: no municipal/livestock wastewater sample is described in the supplied main text. Treat as controlled synthetic-water evidence, not real-wastewater validation. Article states Supplementary data are available online, but SI was not uploaded.

Adsorbent / material: Purchased rice-straw biochar (RBC) and KOH-treated biochar (KRBC)
Experimental design / conditions: RBC was produced from rice straw at 450 °C. KRBC was made by stirring 10 g RBC in 200 mL of 2 M KOH for 4 h, repeatedly washing with ultrapure water and drying at 60 °C.
Reported result: KOH treatment increased BET area from 109.382 to 130.520 m²/g, pore volume from 0.031 to 0.128 cm³/g (4.13-fold), and average pore diameter from 4.227 to 6.747 nm; pHPZC changed from 3.24 to 3.51.
Value / units: RBC vs KRBC: BET 109.382 vs 130.520 m²/g; pore volume 0.031 vs 0.128 cm³/g; mean pore diameter 4.227 vs 6.747 nm; pHPZC 3.24 vs 3.51
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Modification is alkaline washing/treatment of pre-made char rather than an additional high-temperature activation step. The main text describes purchased antibiotic standards and ultrapure-water preparations; it does not identify a collected livestock-wastewater sample.

Experimental design / conditions: 25 mL of 30 mg/L individual antibiotic solution with 0.08 g biochar (3.2 g/L), shaken in the dark at 25 ± 1 °C and 180 rpm, sampled over 10–2880 min and filtered at 0.22 μm. Experiments were in duplicate. Isotherms used SMT and AMX at 5–50 mg/L and OTC at 5–200 mg/L, sampled after 2880 min.
Reported result: The pH-response plots showed greater SMT uptake by KRBC than RBC; at pH 3 capacities were 6.2 vs 4.3 mg/g. OTC removal was reported >90% over the pH range for both chars. AMX removal by RBC remained below 10% across pH; KRBC performed better.
Value / units: SMT at pH 3: RBC 4.3 mg/g, KRBC 6.2 mg/g; OTC removal >90% in reported pH tests; RBC AMX removal <10%
Model / metric: Reported experimental pH-response / removal data; not fitted isotherm qmax
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Use the metrics as reported for their individual conditions. The study's 'livestock wastewater' framing is not corroborated by actual wastewater sampling in the main-text methods; use the synthetic-solution caveat unless the missing Supplementary Information establishes otherwise.

Experimental design / conditions: Langmuir and Freundlich models were compared over stated concentration ranges; Table 3 lists fitted parameters and R²/RMSE.
Reported result: Langmuir fitted Qm (mg/g): SMT RBC 4.52 (R² 0.944), KRBC 6.47 (0.964); OTC RBC 87.8 (0.739), KRBC 51.7 (0.887); AMX RBC 2.01 (0.870), KRBC 7.67 (0.952). Freundlich fit had the higher R²/lower RMSE for all six comparisons; for OTC, Langmuir fit quality is weak, so its Qm values should not be ranked as observed capacity.
Value / units: Fitted Langmuir Qm and R²: SMT 4.52/6.47; OTC 87.8/51.7; AMX 2.01/7.67 mg/g; Freundlich R²: SMT .988/.991; OTC .851/.925; AMX .983/.984
Model / metric: Model-derived Qm; Freundlich generally better fit per R² and RMSE table
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Do not merge fitted qmax/Qm with observed uptake or use the OTC Langmuir capacities as a cross-study ranking; poor Langmuir fits (especially OTC RBC R²=0.739) make such use unreliable. Supplementary model details are not included in uploaded PDF.

Adsorbent / material: KRBC in multi-solute system; RBC comparison
Experimental design / conditions: Mixture contained SMT, OTC and AMX each at 30 mg/L, biochar dose 3.2 g/L, contact time 48 h at room temperature. Cu2+ and Zn2+ were added at 0.5–5.0 mg/L in related tests.
Reported result: For KRBC multi-antibiotic tests, the authors report capacities of 2.924 mg/g for OTC, 2.222 mg/g for SMT and 0.686 mg/g for AMX. Addition of Cu2+ or Zn2+ maintained or increased adsorption for some antibiotic/material combinations, but the pattern depended on antibiotic and ion concentration.
Value / units: KRBC multi-antibiotic capacities: OTC 2.924, SMT 2.222, AMX 0.686 mg/g; metals 0.5–5.0 mg/L
Model / metric: Reported multi-contaminant batch capacities and factor response
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF p. 7, §3.3, Fig. 6 and main text
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: This is a prepared multi-solute laboratory system, not proof of native livestock wastewater treatment. Authors state the origin of metal–antibiotic synergistic adsorption requires further investigation.

Adsorbent / material: RBC/KRBC; simplified carbon models with –OH, C–O or –COOH groups
Experimental design / conditions: FTIR characterization and density-functional-theory calculations compare antibiotic interaction with simplified carbon models carrying different oxygen-containing groups.
Reported result: The paper interprets increased calculated binding energies with –OH groups and FTIR changes as evidence that –OH groups are important adsorption sites. Authors also conclude the mechanism may be chemisorption/heterogeneous, but these are interpretations based on model fits and simplified computational structures.
Value / units: Qualitative mechanistic conclusion; calculated interaction energies appear in Table 4
Model / metric: DFT model interaction energies plus FTIR; not direct measurement of mechanism contribution
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Do not equate a pseudo-second-order fit or simplified DFT binding energy with proof of a single real-solution mechanism. Main-text evidence of real livestock wastewater sampling is absent; supplementary data are referenced but were not uploaded.

Target / co-contaminant: Multiple pharmaceuticals; antibiotic subset includes azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, metronidazole, piperacillin, roxithromycin, sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim
Adsorbent / material: Magnetite-modified pine bark (MPB), commercial biochar (BC) and activated carbon (AC)
Continuum stage: Cross-cutting real-water application; MPB is a modified natural biomass sorbent, not biochar
Experimental design / conditions: Pine bark was dried/sieved (250–500 μm for batch/small columns; 500–1000 μm pilot). Fe(III):Fe(II)=2:1 salts were added and pH adjusted to 9–10 with 1 M NaOH; mixture heated 3 h, then MPB separated, washed to neutral pH and dried.
Reported result: The study tests a magnetite–pine-bark biosorbent with real membrane-bioreactor effluent. Pilot-scale beds use BC + MPB rather than MPB alone, so pilot removal cannot be attributed to MPB alone.
Value / units: Fe(III):Fe(II)=2:1; pH 9–10; 3 h modification; 250–500 / 500–1000 μm particle fractions
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Relevant as cross-cutting application and cost/operation evidence, not a directly comparable biochar qmax study. MBR pretreatment means pharmaceuticals were already present at very low concentrations; study is broader than antibiotics alone.

Target / co-contaminant: Azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, metronidazole, piperacillin, roxithromycin, sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim
Adsorbent / material: MPB vs BC vs AC in actual municipal MBR effluent
Evidence domain: Batch adsorption with real wastewater effluent
Experimental design / conditions: 1.35 g sorbent in 450 mL MBR effluent (3 g/L), shaken at 200 rpm for 3 h, centrifuged at 2500 rpm for 15 min; duplicate experiments.
Reported result: Table 2 reports antibiotic-specific removal percentages: MPB vs BC vs AC respectively — azithromycin 75.6/11.5/87.2%; clarithromycin 33.3/0/33.3%; clindamycin 21.4/14.3/92.9%; metronidazole 12.5/12.5/87.5%; sulfadiazine 28.5/16.6/76.2%; sulfamethoxazole 64.8/31.5/81.5%; trimethoprim 82.2/12.2/98.5%. Piperacillin: MPB 58.1%, while BC outlet concentration exceeded feed and no BC removal percentage is provided.
Value / units: Antibiotic removal (%) by MPB/BC/AC: azithromycin 75.6/11.5/87.2; clarithromycin 33.3/0/33.3; clindamycin 21.4/14.3/92.9; metronidazole 12.5/12.5/87.5; sulfadiazine 28.5/16.6/76.2; sulfamethoxazole 64.8/31.5/81.5; trimethoprim 82.2/12.2/98.5
Model / metric: Reported batch removal efficiencies from real MBR effluent; concentration basis in μg/L
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Matrix is genuine municipal MBR effluent but already biologically treated and pharmaceutical concentrations are very low. Do not assume findings apply to raw wastewater or compare directly to high-concentration synthetic batch capacities.

Target / co-contaminant: Pharmaceutical mixture with antibiotic subset above
Adsorbent / material: Small columns: BC+AC reference vs BC+MPB
Experimental design / conditions: 33-day study; four columns, empty/bed volume reported 791.28 cm³. Columns A1/A2 contained BC (145 g)+AC (20 g); B3/B4 contained BC (145 g)+MPB (20 g). Average flows A1 0.83, A2 0.88, B3 1.26 and B4 1.15 mL/min; contact times 16, 15, 10.5 and 11.5 h. Beds regenerated with 1 M NaOH for 48 h after 13 days then tap-water washed 24 h.
Reported result: Different flow/contact times arose from bed porosity/bacterial occupancy differences. Small columns therefore provide operationally meaningful but not fully matched head-to-head conditions.
Value / units: 791.28 cm³ bed volume; 33 days; flows 0.83–1.26 mL/min; EBCT/contact 10.5–16 h
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Comparison mixes BC with AC or MPB; it is not pure MPB vs pure BC. Contact times and flows differ between columns, so do not rank sorbents without the original study caveats.

Target / co-contaminant: Azithromycin, clarithromycin, clindamycin, metronidazole, sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim
Adsorbent / material: Pilot bed: BC (2.25 kg)+MPB (0.5 kg) in lower bed plus BC (0.78 kg) upper layer
Experimental design / conditions: Pilot column empty-bed volume 21 L, about 120 cm long and 15 cm diameter; run for almost four months (September–December 2023), average flow ~0.90 L/h and contact time about 24 h. Regenerated after ~2 months using 46 L of 0.2 M NaOH for 48 h and then 25 L tap water for 24 h.
Reported result: Table 3 reports average pilot-column removal percentages of azithromycin 92.3%, clarithromycin 71.4%, clindamycin 86.7%, metronidazole 45.9%, sulfadiazine 38.6%, sulfamethoxazole 58.3%, trimethoprim 99.7%. The paper reports 76.5% average removal across all pharmaceuticals overall, not an antibiotic-only average.
Value / units: 21 L empty bed; ~0.90 L/h; ~24 h contact; ~4 months; antibiotic removal % as stated
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Pilot results are for the BC+MPB packed-bed configuration, not MPB alone. Many analytes are close to/below detection after MBR treatment; a minority of summary means use maximum-likelihood estimates when concentrations were below detection. The all-pharmaceutical 76.5% must not be described as antibiotic-only removal.

Target / co-contaminant: Trimethoprim and other pharmaceuticals; microbial and effluent response
Evidence domain: Regeneration, iron leaching and biological effects
Experimental design / conditions: Small-column beds regenerated after day 13 with 1 M NaOH for 48 h plus 24 h tap-water rinse. Pilot bed regenerated after about two months using 46 L 0.2 M NaOH for 48 h plus 25 L tap water for 24 h.
Reported result: Pilot wash effluent contained 1500 μg/L iron after 24 h and 2500 μg/L after 48 h of NaOH washing. Regeneration caused short-time inhibition/toxicity in the Nitrosomonas europaea bioreporter and increased bacterial counts in treated water, attributed to desorption of bacteria from the bed.
Value / units: Fe in pilot wash effluent: 1500 μg/L after 24 h, 2500 μg/L after 48 h; toxicity pulse after regeneration reported qualitatively
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Regeneration is not automatically a net benefit: caustic use, rinse water, iron-containing effluent and transient toxicity need to be included in reuse and safety evaluation.

Adsorbent / material: Magnetite-modified pine bark (MPB) vs commercial activated carbon (AC)
Experimental design / conditions: Authors estimated pine bark at 0.2–0.3 €/kg, milling 0.0038–0.0126 €/kg, chemicals (iron salts and 1 M NaOH) about 1.0667 €/kg MPB, modification at 70 °C for 3 h with estimated cost 0.11512 €/kg and drying at 60 °C for 24 h with cost 0.04045 €/kg.
Reported result: Estimated MPB price: 1.43–1.53 €/kg versus AC at about 3.30 €/kg purchased by the authors. The paper explicitly notes logistics and availability influence costs and states a full sustainability comparison/LCA should be done.
Value / units: MPB 1.43–1.53 €/kg; AC approx. 3.30 €/kg; processing input estimates as above
Model / metric: Author-estimated adsorbent price, not cost per treated water volume or full TEA/LCA
Source location (PDF page; table/figure): PDF pp. 11–12; §3.8; Table S6/S7 referenced but not supplied
Evidence status: Full text reviewed; staged, not yet consolidated
Caveat / follow-up: Do not conclude lower total treatment cost or better life-cycle impact: full LCA is not performed, operational costs/service life/spent media are incomplete, and the AC comparison uses specific Finnish prices and assumptions.
